decomposition.note: March simply contains three more collection days than February. No performance change of any kind.

decomposition.component: equals: true change in daily collection rate
decomposition.note: The entire genuine movement, and it is inside daily noise.

findings.title: Re-ingested payment rows (identical on every business column)
findings.evidence: 486 surplus rows across 486 payment_ids; each is byte-identical to an earlier row on all 8 business columns.
findings.so_what: Genuine double-count. These must be removed or reported recovery is overstated.

findings.title: payment_reference is NOT a unique key -- deduplicating on it destroys real payments
findings.evidence: 3745 references repeat across 8042 rows. 3407 of those references (7366 rows) point at different accounts, different amounts AND different timestamps -- they are distinct payments with a colliding reference. A further 382 rows carry a BLANK reference and would collapse into a single bogus group. Applying that rule would DELETE 4678 rows, of which only 500 are genuine duplicates -- destroying 4178 legitimate payments worth Rs 25.01 Cr of successful collections.
findings.so_what: The obvious cleaning rule is a trap. Dedup on payment_reference and you delete thousands of legitimate payments, then conclude recovery is far worse than it is.

findings.title: Suspected operational double-charges (same account, same amount, <24h apart)
findings.evidence: 0 candidate pairs found on distinct payment_ids.
findings.so_what: Distinct from re-ingestion: identifiers differ, so this is a billing/operations issue rather than a pipeline issue.

findings.title: Payments carry no campaign or interaction key -- all channel attribution is inferred
findings.evidence: payments has 12 columns and none links to a campaign, call or message. calls is the only fact table carrying campaign_id (91350 of 91350 rows populated).
findings.so_what: Channel ROI numbers in existing reporting are the output of an undocumented attribution rule. They cannot be reproduced or audited.

findings.title: Attribution window choice swings credited recovery by a factor of several
findings.evidence: Same payments, last-touch rule, four windows: 1d -> 1.39% (Rs 1.8 Cr); 7d -> 8.99% (Rs 12.2 Cr); 30d -> 31.63% (Rs 42.5 Cr); 90d -> 59.44% (Rs 79.5 Cr)
findings.so_what: Nobody can validate a channel ROI claim without being told the attribution window. Changing it silently changes the answer.

findings.title: Declared timezones are real and misfile calls across day and month boundaries
findings.evidence: 8924 of 91350 calls (9.8%) fall on a different calendar DAY once the declared timezone is applied; 310 cross a MONTH boundary. Zone mix: Asia/Dubai=30464, Asia/Kolkata=30485, UTC=30401.
findings.so_what: Daily operational reports are wrong for roughly a fifth of calls. Month-end numbers move.

findings.title: Call volume is uniform across all 24 hours -- "calling time" cannot be analysed
findings.evidence: Hourly call counts range 3665 to 3964 against a flat expectation of 3806 (max deviation 7.9%). Answer rate by hour ranges 18.78% to 21.35%.
findings.so_what: The brief asks us to investigate calling time as a driver. There is no diurnal pattern to find -- any "best hour" recommendation from this data would be fabricated from noise.

findings.title: Disposition schema versions did NOT change over time -- they coexist throughout
findings.evidence: All 3 versions are present in every one of the 8 months, in near-equal volume (legacy=11726, v1=11620, v2=11654). A genuine migration would show versions succeeding one another; these run in parallel end to end.
findings.so_what: A plausible-sounding explanation for the trend that turns out to be false. Reporting it as a cause would have been wrong.

findings.title: Two disposition codes mean the same thing and coexist in every version
findings.evidence: PTP and PROMISE_TO_PAY both appear in all versions (legacy: PTP=1296 / PROMISE_TO_PAY=1332; v1: PTP=1285 / PROMISE_TO_PAY=1309; v2: PTP=1323 / PROMISE_TO_PAY=1285). Counting only one undercounts promises by 50.1%.
findings.so_what: Any PTP-rate metric filtering on a single code silently halves the numerator. This is the kind of error that survives for years.

findings.title: The agents dimension has no resolvable identity -- it is unusable for attribute analysis
findings.evidence: 30000 rows resolve to only 1000 agent_ids, 1099 employee_codes and just 10 distinct names across 5 teams. A single agent_id carries 9.5 different names on average; a single name maps to 948.9 different agent_ids. The relationship is many-to-many in both directions.
findings.so_what: Agent tenure, team and vendor analysis -- all named in the brief -- cannot be performed. agent_id remains valid as a behavioural key; every attribute hanging off it does not.

findings.title: Calls with a blank agent_id
findings.evidence: 1827 calls (2.00%) carry an empty agent_id and cannot be attributed to any agent.
findings.so_what: Agent-level denominators are short by this amount unless the blanks are handled explicitly.

findings.title: Portfolio mix did NOT change -- it is stable to within a percentage point
findings.evidence: Across the seven complete months, HIGH-risk share moves only 24.68 to 25.65% and mean DPD only 55.87 to 56.90 days. No acquisition, no re-segmentation.
findings.so_what: Mix shift is the most common real-world explanation for a jump like this. Here it is ruled out, which strengthens the calendar explanation.

findings.title: No accounts were originated during the observation window
findings.evidence: All 30000 accounts were opened between 2024-01-01 and 2025-11-30 -- entirely before the 2026-01-01 observation window. The portfolio is a closed cohort.
findings.so_what: A closed cohort should show recovery DECAY over time as collectable accounts are exhausted. Flat performance is therefore mildly negative news, not neutral.

findings.title: The contactable population is NOT shrinking -- no denominator manipulation detected
findings.evidence: Distinct accounts contacted per month ranges 9526 to 10414, and per-day it ranges 331.8 to 340.2 -- flat once month length is removed. Unsuccessful accounts are not disappearing from the base.
findings.so_what: Denominator shrinkage is the classic way a conversion rate is inflated. Ruled out here -- which again points back to the calendar.

findings.title: Status history contains events recorded BEFORE they occurred
findings.evidence: 30191 of 60000 history rows have recorded_at earlier than event_at (impossible). Ingest lag ranges to 24 hours. 18952 accounts carry contradictory status sequences.
findings.so_what: Point-in-time reconstruction of account state is unreliable. Any as-of-date report built on this table can silently disagree with itself.

findings.title: The accounts table disagrees with its own status history
findings.evidence: 26296 of 30000 accounts (87.7%) have a current status in accounts that does not match the most recent event in account_status_history.
findings.so_what: There is no single source of truth for account status. Which table you join to changes your answer -- exactly the situation the brief warns about.

findings.title: Fact tables reference borrowers that do not exist in the borrower table
findings.evidence: 7109 of 86757 calls (8.19%) and 1973 of 24058 payments (8.20%) carry a borrower_id absent from the borrower dimension. 985 distinct borrower_ids appear in fact tables but never in borrowers.csv at all -- a referential break present in the SOURCE data, not introduced by cleaning.
findings.so_what: Any borrower-level cut -- geography, contactability, borrower segment -- silently drops ~8% of activity. The rows are retained and flagged rather than filtered, so the loss is visible instead of invisible.

metric_definitions.problem: Counts CALL rows, but a single outreach attempt can produce several call rows and 120,000 call_attempts sit behind 90,000 calls. It also treats a borrower reached ten times as ten contacts, so the metric rises when the dialler gets more aggressive even if no new person is reached.
metric_definitions.our_defn: distinct accounts reached at least once in the period / distinct accounts attempted in the period. Account-level, not event-level, so it cannot be inflated by redialling.

metric_definitions.business_defn: calls with a "contact" disposition / calls placed
metric_definitions.problem: There is no field identifying whether the party reached was the borrower. WRONG_NUMBER is one of nine disposition codes and is assigned independently of call_status: FAILED 21.2%, BUSY 20.1%, NO_ANSWER 20.1%, ANSWERED 19.5%, VOICEMAIL 19.2%. At least 61.3% of WRONG_NUMBER dispositions sit on calls that never connected, where a wrong-number determination is impossible.
metric_definitions.our_defn: Not computable from this data. We report answered-call rate instead and state plainly that true RPC requires a party-identification field that does not exist.

metric_definitions.business_defn: dispositions where code = PTP / total dispositions
metric_definitions.problem: PTP and PROMISE_TO_PAY are separate codes for the same concept, present in every schema version. Filtering on either one alone undercounts promises by roughly 50%.
metric_definitions.our_defn: dispositions where code IN (PTP, PROMISE_TO_PAY) / distinct accounts contacted. Synonyms collapsed at the clean layer so the error cannot recur downstream.

metric_definitions.business_defn: promises with status = KEPT / total promises
metric_definitions.problem: The status field does not correspond to reality. A promise marked KEPT is followed by an actual payment within 30 days 7.75% of the time; one marked BROKEN, 6.63%. The field carries essentially no information about whether money arrived.
metric_definitions.our_defn: Ignore the status field entirely. Measure fulfilment directly: promises followed by a successful payment of at least the promised amount within 30 days / total promises.

metric_definitions.business_defn: sum of payment amounts in the month / opening outstanding
metric_definitions.problem: Includes FAILED, PENDING and REVERSED payments; and the monthly numerator makes a 31-day month look 11% better than a 28-day one.
metric_definitions.our_defn: Net collections per day = (SUCCESS - REVERSED) / days in period. Day-normalised and net of money that left again.

metric_definitions.problem: The denominator silently changes as accounts close or are written off, so the ratio can rise with no extra rupee collected.
metric_definitions.our_defn: Net collections per day / accounts in the fixed opening cohort. The cohort is frozen at window start, so the denominator cannot drift.

metric_definitions.problem: agent_sessions has no reliable link to outcomes, and the agents dimension cannot resolve identity, so hours cannot be attributed to a person or team with confidence.
metric_definitions.our_defn: Computed at portfolio level only, from summed session hours. Never broken down by agent, team or vendor -- those cuts are not supportable.

metric_definitions.business_defn: channel cost / amount attributed to that channel
metric_definitions.problem: No cost data exists in the extract, and the attributed amount depends entirely on an unstated attribution window: across all four channels, last-touch credit covers 3.2% of successful payments at 1 day, 20.2% at 7 days, 59.8% at 30 days and 83.8% at 90 days -- a 26x swing from the window choice alone.
metric_definitions.our_defn: Not computable. We report the attribution sensitivity instead, so the reader can see how much any such figure would move.

metric_definitions.business_defn: accounts that paid after a channel touch / accounts touched
metric_definitions.problem: Every account is touched on several channels, so the denominators overlap and the shares sum to far more than 100%. It also conflates correlation with causation -- untouched accounts pay at nearly the same rate.
metric_definitions.our_defn: Reported only as a comparison against the never-contacted baseline, with a confidence interval on the difference. Absolute per-channel conversion is not reported at all.

metric_definitions.business_defn: this month total / last month total - 1
metric_definitions.problem: Confounded with month length. February to March carries a mechanical +10.71% before any performance change whatsoever.
metric_definitions.our_defn: Day-normalised rate change, with a 95% confidence interval from the daily series. Monthly totals are never compared directly.

simpsons.note: Strict Simpson's paradox is NOT present: no month-pair shows the aggregate moving opposite to every subgroup. What IS present is a month-length confound: segments whose Feb->Mar growth fell below the +10.71% calendar effect appear positive in totals and negative per day. That is a normalisation artefact, not an aggregation paradox, and must not be labelled Simpson's.

step1_change_detection.conclusion: No targeting change is observable: strategy versions run concurrently and the targeted population's composition is stable.

counterfactual.verdict: The estimated effect is statistically indistinguishable from zero, so the best estimate of the counterfactual is that recovery would have been the same.
